questions.stem: A cereal label lists 180 kcal per 3/4 cup. A client eats 1.5 cups. How many calories come from the cereal?
questions.rationale: There are two servings: 1.5 ÷ 0.75 = 2; 2 × 180 = 360 kcal. The other answers do not multiply by the amount consumed.

questions.stem: Two soups have the same serving size. Soup A provides 8% DV sodium and soup B provides 22% DV. Which statement is accurate?
options: Soup B is high in sodium per serving by the FDA general %DV guide.
Both soups are low in sodium by the 5% DV guide.
The percentages cannot be compared when serving sizes match.
questions.rationale: Under the general FDA guide, 20% DV or more is high and 5% DV or less is low. Soup A has less sodium, but 8% is neither zero nor within the 5% low reference. Equal serving sizes allow comparison.

questions.stem: A label lists total sugars 12 g, including 7 g added sugars, per serving. How much total sugar is present in two servings?
questions.rationale: Total sugar is 12 × 2 = 24 g. Added sugars are already included in total sugars; do not add them again. The two servings contain 14 g added sugars.

questions.stem: Which addition can enhance absorption of nonheme iron from a bean meal?
options: A food chosen only for its saturated fat content
questions.rationale: Vitamin C enhances nonheme iron absorption. Saturated fat does not provide that mechanism; removing the iron source or fruits and vegetables is not the strategy described.

questions.stem: After explaining a new meal-planning method, which question best checks understanding using teach-back?
options: Can you explain how you would plan tomorrow's lunch so I can check how clearly I explained it?
Please memorize every sentence in the handout.
questions.rationale: Teach-back asks the person to explain in their own words and makes the professional responsible for clarity. Yes/no questions do not demonstrate application; repeating memorized phrases does not verify understanding.

questions.stem: During teach-back, a patient describes the plan incorrectly. What should the RD do next?
options: Repeat the identical wording more loudly.
Explain the point another way, then check understanding again.
questions.rationale: AHRQ recommends clarifying and checking again. A misunderstanding does not prove nonadherence; raising one’s voice or omitting the information does not resolve it.

questions.stem: Which patient-selected goal is most specific and measurable?
options: Add one serving of vegetables to dinner on four days this week and record it.
questions.rationale: The goal specifies an observable action, frequency, and time frame. The other choices are vague or absolute and lack a practical measure. The goal must also be realistic for the person.

questions.stem: Investigators randomly assign adults to counseling program A or B and compare outcomes after 12 weeks. What is the design?
questions.rationale: Random assignment to interventions defines a randomized trial. A case-control study selects by outcome; a cross-sectional study measures at a point or period; a case report does not compare randomized groups.

questions.stem: Investigators enroll people with and without a foodborne illness, then compare prior food exposures. What is the design?
questions.rationale: Selection starts with the outcome (ill or not ill), followed by comparison of prior exposures: a case-control study. No randomization or assigned intervention is described.

questions.stem: In a defined group of 100 event attendees, 20 of 50 people who ate dish X became ill, compared with 5 of 50 who did not. What is the risk ratio?
questions.rationale: Exposed risk = 20/50 = 0.40; unexposed risk = 5/50 = 0.10; risk ratio = 4. Do not divide only overall totals or reverse the groups. This observed association alone does not prove causation.

questions.stem: A one-time survey finds that frequent breakfast eaters report better health. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: Breakfast caused better health in every participant.
An association was observed; this design alone does not establish that breakfast caused better health.
The survey proves that all other behaviors were identical.
questions.rationale: A cross-sectional association alone does not establish temporal direction or causation. No randomization is described, and other factors may differ between groups.

questions.stem: A team follows initially disease-free adults with different naturally occurring dietary exposures and records new disease over time. What design is described?
options: Case-control study selected by existing disease
questions.rationale: A cohort follows groups defined by exposure and records new outcomes. Naturally occurring exposure is not random assignment; selection did not begin with existing cases.

questions.stem: An RD wants to compare sodium in two breads. Bread A lists 180 mg per 30 g; bread B lists 250 mg per 50 g. Which has less sodium per 100 g?
questions.rationale: Standardize the serving: A = 180/30 × 100 = 600 mg; B = 250/50 × 100 = 500 mg. Comparing 180 with 250 alone ignores different serving sizes.

questions.stem: An RDN collects a food record, recent laboratory results, and weight history before identifying a nutrition problem. Which NCP step is being performed?
questions.rationale: Gathering and interpreting data is nutrition assessment. Intervention implements a plan; monitoring tracks response; a medical diagnosis is not this NCP step.

questions.stem: Which statement identifies the etiology in this teaching example: "Inadequate intake related to inability to shop for food as evidenced by a three-day intake below the agreed target"?
questions.rationale: The cause is inability to shop for food. Inadequate intake is the problem; intake records are evidence; the goal is the comparator.

questions.stem: Which item is the strongest measurable sign or symptom for a nutrition diagnosis concerning inadequate intake?
options: The client has a medical diagnosis
Documented intake averaging 900 kcal/day against an assessed 1,800 kcal/day target
questions.rationale: Documented intake compared with requirements supports the problem. Personal judgments and general statements are not measurements; a medical diagnosis alone does not demonstrate inadequate intake.

questions.stem: A client can prepare meals but cannot afford the foods in the current plan. What is the best next nutrition intervention?
options: Develop an affordable plan with the client and connect them with appropriate food resources
Repeat the same expensive menu more slowly
questions.rationale: The intervention should address the access barrier. Repeating advice without adaptation does not resolve cost; assuming low motivation is unsupported; abandoning monitoring prevents assessment of response.

questions.stem: After four weeks, the RDN compares the client's average intake with the agreed intake goal. Which NCP step is illustrated?
questions.rationale: Comparing the response with the goal is monitoring and evaluation. Screening identifies risk; diagnosis names the problem; shopping does not describe this action.

questions.stem: A weight entry differs markedly from the previous day, and the record indicates a different scale was used. What should the RDN do first?
options: Prescribe a fixed calorie increase without assessment
Verify the measurement and relevant clinical context
questions.rationale: Checking data quality and context avoids a premature conclusion. Discarding everything or intervening automatically also overlooks the need for consistent assessment.

questions.stem: The goal is to increase average meal intake from 40% to 75% by the next visit. Which indicator most directly evaluates that goal?
questions.rationale: The indicator should match the goal: percentage consumed. Printed material measures activity, not outcome; room and insurance do not measure intake.

questions.stem: Which sequence best represents the four NCP steps?
options: Assessment, diagnosis, intervention, monitoring and evaluation
questions.rationale: The conceptual sequence is assessment, diagnosis, intervention, and monitoring/evaluation; care may return to reassessment. The other sequences mix functions or omit steps.

questions.stem: A client reports a new barrier that makes the original nutrition plan impractical. What is the best response?
options: Reassess the new information and revise the plan as indicated
Keep the plan unchanged because it was documented
End care because the first plan failed
Replace the nutrition diagnosis with the medical diagnosis automatically
questions.rationale: New information calls for reassessment and an informed adjustment. A prior record does not make the plan immutable; ending care or automatically changing the diagnosis does not resolve the barrier.

questions.stem: For this calculation exercise, an agreed energy target is 2,000 kcal/day and documented intake is 1,500 kcal/day. What percentage of the target was consumed?
questions.rationale: 1,500 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 75%. The other options use incorrect relationships; 133% reverses numerator and denominator. The target was supplied, not prescribed by the exercise.

questions.stem: A prescribed enteral formula provides 1.5 kcal/mL. For this exercise, 1,200 mL is actually delivered. How much energy is delivered?
questions.rationale: 1,200 mL × 1.5 kcal/mL = 1,800 kcal. 800 comes from dividing incorrectly; 1,200 ignores density; 1,500 does not use the supplied volume.

questions.stem: A prescribed formula provides 1.2 kcal/mL. What volume supplies the stated target of 1,800 kcal?
questions.rationale: Volume = 1,800 kcal ÷ 1.2 kcal/mL = 1,500 mL. Multiplication gives 2,160; 1,800 ignores density; 600 does not satisfy the supplied relationship.

questions.stem: A prescribed daily volume is 1,440 mL. Feeding is planned for 18 hours, with no additional interruption in this exercise. What hourly rate delivers that volume?
questions.rationale: 1,440 ÷ 18 = 80 mL/h. 60 assumes 24 hours; 100 and 120 would deliver more than the prescribed volume in the stated time.

questions.stem: A client weighed 80 kg at baseline and now weighs 76 kg. What is the percentage weight loss relative to baseline?
questions.rationale: (80 − 76) ÷ 80 × 100 = 5%. Four is the difference in kg; 5.3% uses current weight as denominator; 95% is the fraction retained. This alone does not diagnose malnutrition.

questions.stem: For this exercise, a prescribed protein target is 1.2 g/kg/day using a specified calculation weight of 70 kg. What is the daily target?
questions.rationale: 1.2 × 70 = 84 g/day. 58 results from division; 70 ignores the factor; 72 uses a different weight. The factor is supplied for the exercise, not a universal prescription.

questions.stem: A soup label lists 360 mg sodium per 1-cup serving. A client consumes 1.5 cups. How much sodium does this provide?
questions.rationale: 360 × 1.5 = 540 mg. Division gives 240; 360 is one serving; 720 is two.

questions.stem: A package lists 2.5 servings per container and 160 kcal per serving. If the entire package is consumed, what is the energy intake?
questions.rationale: 2.5 × 160 = 400 kcal. 320 uses two servings; 160 uses one; 640 uses four.

questions.stem: A client reads "Total Sugars 12 g, Includes 5 g Added Sugars" for one serving. Which interpretation is correct?
options: All 12 g are necessarily added sugars
The 5 g added sugars are included within the 12 g total sugars
The serving contains 17 g total sugars
The label gives no information about added sugars
questions.rationale: The 5 g of added sugars are already included in the 12 g total. Adding them double-counts; total does not mean entirely added, and the information is provided.

questions.stem: A client with CKD asks whether every person with CKD must follow the same potassium restriction. What is the best response?
options: The plan should reflect individual potassium levels, needs, and treatment context
All patients must eliminate every fruit
A food is safe regardless of portion size
questions.rationale: The plan must be individualized; portion sizes matter. Eliminating all fruit is excessive, needs can change, and quantity changes potassium intake.

questions.stem: A client whose care plan limits potassium wants to replace table salt with a potassium-chloride salt substitute. What is the best advice?
options: Use unlimited amounts because it is not sodium chloride
Assume all salt substitutes contain no minerals
Check the ingredient list and discuss its potassium contribution with the care team before using it
Stop all prescribed medicines to compensate
questions.rationale: Potassium chloride adds potassium and must fit the care plan. The other choices ignore composition or propose an unsupported medication change.

questions.stem: A client with confirmed celiac disease is choosing a side dish. Which plain ingredient is naturally gluten-free?
questions.rationale: Plain rice is naturally gluten-free. Barley, rye, and semolina (wheat) contain gluten. Preparation and cross-contact must still be checked.

questions.stem: A restaurant offers a gluten-free meal but prepares it with utensils contaminated by wheat flour. Which concern should the RDN identify?
questions.rationale: Contaminated utensils can transfer gluten to the meal. Sugar, color, and protein do not address the described risk.

questions.stem: A pregnant client asks about a U.S. program offering supplemental foods, nutrition education, and referrals. Which is the most appropriate program to explore, subject to eligibility review?
options: Medicare as a universal grocery program
questions.rationale: WIC serves pregnant people and other categories, with residence, income, and nutritional-risk criteria. Referral does not guarantee approval; the other options do not provide this program.

questions.stem: A community project reports that 72 of 240 surveyed households met its stated food-insecurity criterion. What percentage met that criterion?
questions.rationale: 72 ÷ 240 × 100 = 30%. 72 is a count, not a percentage; 33 and 40 do not follow from the data. The criterion was supplied in the fictional study.

questions.stem: A nutrition program aims to improve intake. Which result is an outcome rather than simply an activity count?
options: Change in participants' measured intake relative to the program goal
questions.rationale: Change in intake relative to the goal measures an outcome. Handouts, emails, and chairs describe activities or resources, not a nutrition effect.

questions.stem: A diet history contains "one bowl of cereal," but the bowl size is unknown. What is the best next assessment action?
options: Clarify the portion using a measurement aid or household measure
Assume it equals the label serving
questions.rationale: Clarifying portion size improves the estimate. A bowl does not necessarily equal a label serving; entering zero or diagnosing without data creates error.

questions.stem: A follow-up measure improved but remains below the agreed goal. What is the best interpretation?
options: There is partial progress; reassess barriers and continue or adjust the plan
The baseline data are no longer useful
The intervention must be stopped immediately
questions.rationale: Improvement below the goal indicates partial progress. It is not complete success and does not automatically require stopping; the baseline still permits comparison.

questions.stem: A department schedules 240 paid labor hours per week. In this organization, one full-time equivalent (FTE) equals 40 paid hours per week. How many FTEs are scheduled?
questions.rationale: FTE = 240/40 = 6. Do not confuse headcount with full-time equivalents: different combinations of employees can total 6 FTEs. The other answers do not match the stated division.

questions.stem: A cafeteria produces 600 meals using 120 productive labor hours. What is its productivity in meals per labor hour?
questions.rationale: 600/120 = 5 meals per labor hour. 0.2 is the inverse (hours per meal); 20 and 72 do not represent this ratio. The requested unit determines the numerator.

questions.stem: Monthly food sales are $20,000 and the cost of food sold is $7,000. Define food cost percentage as food cost divided by food sales, multiplied by 100. What is the food cost percentage?
questions.rationale: 7,000/20,000 × 100 = 35%. The 65% is the portion of sales remaining after this cost, not food cost percentage; the other choices do not apply the definition.

questions.stem: A single-product lunch service has monthly fixed costs of $3,600. Each lunch sells for $12 and has a variable cost of $6. Assuming constant prices and costs, how many lunches must be sold monthly to break even?
questions.rationale: Unit contribution margin = 12 − 6 = $6; break-even = 3,600/6 = 600 lunches. Dividing by price ignores variable cost. The other quantities do not equate revenue with costs.

questions.stem: A service sells 800 identical lunches at $12 each. Variable cost is $6 per lunch and monthly fixed costs are $3,600. There are no other costs or revenues. What is monthly profit?
questions.rationale: Revenue = 800 × 12 = $9,600; variable cost = $4,800; profit = $9,600 − $4,800 − $3,600 = $1,200. $4,800 is contribution before fixed costs; $9,600 is revenue, not profit.

questions.stem: A department budgeted $4,000 for supplies and spent $4,600 for the same period. Define expense variance as actual minus budget. What is the variance?
questions.rationale: $4,600 − $4,000 = $600 over budget: an unfavorable expense variance, not a saving. The variance is the difference, not the total budgeted or spent.

questions.stem: A flexible food budget allows $3 per meal. Actual volume is 1,400 meals and actual food cost is $4,500. What is the actual cost above the flexible allowance?
questions.rationale: Flexible budget = 1,400 × $3 = $4,200. Excess = $4,500 − $4,200 = $300. Comparing with a different volume would distort the evaluation.

questions.stem: A manager defines annual employee turnover as separations during the year divided by average headcount, multiplied by 100. There were 6 separations and an average headcount of 40. What is turnover?
questions.rationale: 6/40 × 100 = 15%. Separations are counts, not automatically percentages; 40 is the denominator. The question supplies the definition because turnover metrics vary.

questions.stem: A quality-improvement team plans to test a revised tray-check procedure. Which action best represents a small initial test of change?
options: Test it on one unit for one lunch period and record results
Implement it hospital-wide permanently without measurements
Replace all employees before testing it
Wait until errors disappear on their own
questions.rationale: A small test allows results to be observed and adjustments made before expansion. Permanent implementation without measurement prevents learning; replacing the whole team does not test the procedure; waiting is not a change test.

questions.stem: During a tray-check pilot, the team records error rates and compares the findings with its prediction. Which PDSA phase is represented by analyzing those results?
questions.rationale: Study analyzes results and compares them with the prediction. Plan defines the test; Do carries it out; Act uses learning to adapt, adopt, or abandon the change. Measurement during execution and subsequent analysis are related but distinct.

questions.stem: Before a conditional job offer, which interview question is generally appropriate under EEOC guidance?
options: What prescription medications do you take?
Can you perform the essential job duties, with or without reasonable accommodation?
What is the severity of your medical condition?
questions.rationale: An interview may address ability to perform job functions. Pre-offer questions about medications, disability, or severity seek medical information inappropriate in this context. Specific rules apply at later stages and for accommodations.

questions.stem: A manager wants a measurable objective for reducing tray errors. Which statement best specifies an outcome and a deadline?
options: Reduce tray errors from 8 per 100 trays to 4 per 100 trays within 8 weeks
questions.rationale: The correct objective states a measure, starting point, target, and time frame. The others do not permit objective verification. This is an objective-writing exercise; it does not establish feasibility without process analysis.

questions.stem: A service recorded 18 incorrect trays among 600 trays checked before an intervention and 9 among 600 afterward. What happened to the observed error rate?
questions.rationale: 18/600 = 3%; 9/600 = 1.5%. The absolute reduction is 1.5 percentage points and the relative reduction is 50%. These observed data alone do not establish causation or statistical significance.

questions.stem: Under the FDA Food Code 2022 cooling provisions for cooked TCS food, which schedule meets BOTH required cooling limits?
options: 135°F to 70°F in 3 hours, then to 41°F by hour 6
135°F to 70°F in 2 hours, then to 41°F after 8 hours total
135°F to 70°F in 2 hours, then to 41°F by hour 6 total
135°F to 90°F in 2 hours, then to 41°F by hour 6
questions.rationale: Cooling must reach 70°F from 135°F within 2 hours and 41°F from 135°F within 6 hours total. The correct answer meets both; the others fail the first stage or the total. Section 3-501.14.

questions.stem: Which method is appropriate for accelerating the cooling of a large batch of cooked soup under the FDA Food Code?
options: Leave the soup in one deep stockpot at room temperature overnight
Divide it into shallow pans and monitor time and temperature
Seal it tightly in a large insulated container
Wait until it smells different before refrigerating
questions.rationale: Dividing food into shallow containers improves heat transfer, with monitoring of the limits. Deep or insulating containers slow cooling; smell is not a safety criterion. Section 3-501.15.

questions.stem: Under the FDA Food Code 2022, which temperatures meet the usual hot- and cold-holding limits for TCS food, excluding specified exceptions and time-as-control procedures?
questions.rationale: The usual holding limits are at least 135°F hot and at most 41°F cold. The correct answer meets both; the others fail at least one. Section 3-501.16.

questions.stem: A recipe needs 12 lb of edible, trimmed produce. The stated edible yield is 80% of purchased weight. How much untrimmed produce must be purchased?
questions.rationale: Purchase weight = 12/0.80 = 15 lb. Multiplying by 0.80 would give usable weight from 12 lb purchased, not the purchase required. The other values do not supply 12 lb usable at this yield.

questions.stem: A purchase unit yields 24 portions at the required serving size. How many whole purchase units are needed for 130 portions, with no additional buffer?
questions.rationale: 130/24 = 5.4167 units; whole units must be rounded up to 6. Five yield only 120 portions; 5.4 is not a whole unit; 7 exceeds the minimum.

questions.stem: A standardized recipe yields 40 portions and uses 3 lb of rice. Assuming all ingredients scale proportionally, how much rice is required for 100 portions?
questions.rationale: Scaling factor = 100/40 = 2.5. Rice = 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 lb. Portion size remains unchanged; the other quantities do not apply the correct factor.

questions.stem: A food-contact surface has just been used for a food containing milk. Before preparing a milk-free special order on that surface, which action best reduces allergen cross-contact?
options: Remove only the visible crumbs with a dry towel
Apply sanitizer over food residue without cleaning
Assume cooking the next food will eliminate the milk allergen
Use the established effective wash-rinse-sanitize-air-dry procedure and clean utensils
questions.rationale: Effective cleaning followed by the sanitizing procedure and clean utensils reduces allergen transfer. Removing only visible residue or sanitizing without cleaning is not equivalent; cooking does not guarantee allergen elimination.

lessons.title: Principles: Labels, Communication, and Evidence
lessons.text:
Labels: Start with the serving size and the number of servings consumed. Multiply nutrients and calories by the serving factor. Added sugars are included in total sugars; do not add them twice. Compare equivalent portions. As a general % Daily Value guide, 5% DV or less is low and 20% DV or more is high. Example: 120 mg per 40 g equals 300 mg per 100 g.
Communication: Checking understanding means more than asking whether the person understands. Ask the person to explain or demonstrate the plan, and clarify if needed. Turn intentions into observable actions agreed upon with the person.
Research: In a randomized trial, the researcher assigns interventions by chance; a cohort follows exposures and outcomes; a case-control study selects participants by outcome and compares exposures. Association does not automatically establish causation. Risk = new cases / people at risk; risk ratio = risk in the exposed group / risk in the unexposed group.
Nutrition science: Vitamin C can improve nonheme iron absorption. Do not extrapolate from a mechanism to recommend supplements indiscriminately.

lessons.title: From Data to Decisions: The Nutrition Care Process
lessons.text:
The Nutrition Care Process (NCP) organizes assessment/reassessment, nutrition diagnosis, intervention, and monitoring and evaluation. First identify which step a question asks about. Collecting intake, measurements, and laboratory data is assessment; comparing later results with a goal is monitoring. A PES statement connects the problem, etiology, and signs and symptoms. The etiology should guide an intervention capable of addressing the cause; signs and symptoms should allow progress to be monitored. A medical diagnosis does not replace a nutrition diagnosis.
Example: If intake fell because a person has difficulty buying food, teaching expensive recipes does not resolve the barrier. Before choosing an action, find the data supporting the decision. Retrieval question: What information would show whether the intervention worked?
Applied exercise: A person reports losing transportation to the grocery store, and intake has fallen. Use three columns: observed problem, possible cause, and additional data needed. Before attributing the decrease to a lack of knowledge, ask how the person obtains food and what resources are available. Compare repeating a handout with adapting the plan to available access. Explain aloud which addresses the barrier better and why. Then write a follow-up question: How has meal frequency or amount changed? Spend five minutes creating another case with the same problem but a different cause.

lessons.title: Care Calculations: Units Before Formulas
lessons.text:
In this block, prescribed targets and formula concentrations are supplied in the questions; they are exercise data, not universal recommendations. Write the desired unit before calculating. Energy delivered by formula = mL × kcal/mL. Required volume = kcal ÷ kcal/mL. Rate = volume ÷ hours actually available. Adequacy = intake ÷ target × 100. Percentage weight loss = (previous weight − current weight) ÷ previous weight × 100. Do not confuse an arithmetic result with a malnutrition diagnosis; interpretation requires clinical context. Estimate mentally to detect tenfold errors. For labels, multiply values per serving by the number of servings consumed.
Worked example: A stated target of 1,600 kcal using a 1.25 kcal/mL formula requires 1,280 mL. Given over 16 hours, the rate is 80 mL/h. Reverse check: 80 × 16 × 1.25 = 1,600 kcal. Over 20 hours the rate is 64 mL/h; total volume and energy stay the same. Another example: a change from 90 kg to 85.5 kg is a 4.5 kg loss, or 5% of initial weight. Unit check: kcal ÷ kcal/mL leaves mL. Practice before checking: What volume of 2 kcal/mL formula supplies a stated target of 1,700 kcal? Answer: 850 mL. None of these numbers establishes a clinical indication.

lessons.title: Individualize the Intervention and Evaluate the Response
lessons.text:
Choose an action that addresses the demonstrated barrier or risk rather than applying an automatic rule. Needs vary in chronic kidney disease; potassium, protein, and other components require individual assessment. In confirmed celiac disease, avoiding gluten includes recognizing wheat, barley, and rye and preventing cross-contact. In community health, referral is not a guarantee of eligibility: WIC serves specific categories and has additional criteria.
When reviewing a question, ask: Which fact was decisive? Which distractor was tempting, and why does it not answer the case? Define an observable indicator and a comparable follow-up target.
Applied exercise: Choose one of these three contexts and write four lines: missing information, a possible intervention, a monitoring indicator, and a condition requiring reassessment. For kidney disease, do not invent a numeric limit without an individual target. For celiac disease, distinguish an ingredient from the preparation process. For WIC, distinguish a person who may be referred from one whose eligibility has been approved. In the final minutes, turn an incorrect answer into a new question: change one case detail and explain how it changes your choice. This practices transfer of reasoning, not memorization of letters.

lessons.title: Management: Turning Problems into Measures and Decisions
lessons.text:
First define what the question measures and its units. Practice FTE = labor hours / hours per FTE; productivity = meals / productive labor hours; and cost percentage = cost / sales × 100. The exercises state their assumptions. For a single product, contribution margin per unit = price − variable cost; break-even units = fixed cost / contribution margin per unit. Do not confuse revenue, contribution, and profit.
For quality improvement, test a small change, compare results with predictions, and decide what to do next: Plan, Do, Study, Act. An observed improvement alone does not prove causation. In hiring, focus a pre-offer interview on job functions, not a candidate’s diagnosis or medications.
Active practice: Rewrite each formula with units and explain why the most tempting wrong answer is wrong. Worked example: 150 meals / 30 productive hours = 5 meals per hour. If the same team produces 150 meals in 25 hours, the ratio rises to 6 meals per hour; that alone does not prove improved quality or safety. Another check: at a $10 price, $4 variable cost, and $1,800 fixed cost, each sale contributes $6 and 300 sales are needed to break even. Verify: $3,000 revenue − $1,200 variable cost − $1,800 fixed cost = zero profit.

lessons.title: Foodservice: Quantities and Risk Control
lessons.text:
Yield distinguishes as-purchased (AP) quantity from edible-portion (EP) quantity: purchase quantity = usable amount needed ÷ yield fraction. When only whole packages can be purchased, round up. The recipe scaling factor = desired portions ÷ original recipe portions.
The food-safety exercises explicitly use the FDA Food Code 2022, a model adopted differently by jurisdictions. Cool cooked TCS food from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours and to 41°F within 6 hours total; shallow containers help. Usual holding limits are hot at or above 135°F and cold at or below 41°F, subject to exceptions. Allergen cross-contact control requires attention to surfaces, utensils, and cleaning; removing visible residue alone is insufficient. Apply the conditions in the question; appearance or smell cannot replace a safety rule.
Worked example: 18 kg usable at 75% yield requires 18 / 0.75 = 24 kg purchased. Reverse check: 24 × 0.75 = 18 kg. A 20-portion recipe must be multiplied by 3 to make 60 portions of the same size; do not triple the size of each portion. Update: The Food Code 2026 has been published; the basic limits studied here remain the same. The exercises name the 2022 edition explicitly, not as the latest edition.
